statement: How many three-digit numbers have digits that multiply to 12? For example, 341 is one of them.

choices.misconception: I found the three sets of digits, 1-2-6, 1-3-4 and 2-2-3, and forgot that each set can be arranged in several orders.
I missed the digits 1, 3, 4, so I only counted 6 orders of 1, 2, 6 and 3 orders of 2, 2, 3.
I missed the set 2, 2, 3 because I only looked for three different digits.
I counted 6 orders for 2, 2, 3 as well, not noticing that swapping the two 2s gives the same number.

hints: First find which sets of digits work, then count orders.
Split into cases by the set of three digits. Three different digits can be ordered in several ways, but a set with a repeated digit has fewer different orders.
The sets are 1, 2, 6 and 1, 3, 4 and 2, 2, 3. Count the orders of each separately.

solutions.reliable: No digit can be 0, and every digit must divide 12. The sets of three digits with product 12 are 1, 2, 6 and 1, 3, 4 and 2, 2, 3 (1, 1, 12 fails because 12 is not a digit). Three different digits give 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 orders each, so 12 numbers from the first two sets. The set 2, 2, 3 gives only 3 orders: 223, 232, 322. Total 6 + 6 + 3 = 15. The transferable idea: in casework, count each case by its own rule, and watch for repeated items, which reduce the number of orders.

whyOnTest: Casework by digit set, then counting orders, rewards a careful list and punishes mishandling a repeated digit in either direction.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
